subject: Business
title: Razor-and-Blade: Lock In Then Profit
description: A 60-second lesson on Razor-and-Blade: Lock In Then Profit.

hook.text: Gillette sells razors cheaply. Then charges premium prices for blades you'll buy for years.

buildup.text: The razor-and-blade model sells the base product at low margin and profits from consumable refills or add-ons.

discovery.text: Printers, coffee machines (pods), and gaming consoles all use this model.

twist.text: This model creates lock-in. Once you buy a Keurig, you're committed to K-Cup pods. Switching costs keep you paying.

climax.text: Apple reversed the model: premium hardware, cheap/free software. The iPhone is the razor; the App Store is the blade.

punchline.text: Give away the fishing rod. Sell the bait forever.

quiz.question: How does the razor-and-blade model generate profit?
options: Selling the base product cheaply and profiting from consumable refills
Selling both the product and refills at premium prices

details.summary: The razor-and-blade model sells the initial product cheaply or at a loss to lock in customers who must buy proprietary refills or consumables at high margins. Gillette, inkjet printers, and gaming consoles all use this model to generate long-term recurring revenue.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding lock-in models helps both businesses designing pricing strategies and consumers recognizing when low upfront costs will lead to expensive ongoing commitments over the product's lifetime.
takeaways: Sell the base product cheaply to lock in customers for high-margin consumables
Gillette razors, printer ink, and game consoles use this pricing strategy
The model depends on making switching costly through proprietary designs

faq.question: Why is printer ink often more expensive per ounce than perfume?
faq.answer: Printers are sold at or below cost, and manufacturers recover profits through proprietary ink cartridges marked up dramatically. DRM chips prevent third-party refills, maintaining the lock-in. The true cost of printing should include lifetime ink costs, not just the printer price.

faq.question: How are some companies disrupting the razor-and-blade model?
faq.answer: Dollar Shave Club and Harry's disrupted Gillette by offering quality razors at fair prices through subscriptions. Third-party ink cartridges and refill services undermine printer lock-in. Consumers increasingly seek models with transparent total cost of ownership.
